 Tigers to Be Relocated to Buxa Tiger Reserve from Assam and Bihar 
 Star marking (1-5) indicates the importance of topic -->
 Why in News?   
 West Bengal has announced plans to relocate two more tigers from Assam and Bihar to Buxa Tiger Reserve (BTR) by the end of November 2026. The initiative aims to strengthen the reserve's resident tiger population as part of a phased tiger reintroduction and recovery programme.    
 Key Points:   
 Proposed Tiger Relocation   
 Destination: Buxa Tiger Reserve, Alipurduar district, West Bengal.   
 Source states: Assam and Bihar.   
 Number of tigers: Two.   
 Expected timeline: By the end of November 2026.   
 Objective: To strengthen the resident tiger population and establish a viable, breeding and self-sustaining tiger population in Buxa.   
 The relocation programme is being undertaken under the supervision of the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) .   
 Earlier Relocation of a Tigress from Bihar   
 On 2 October 2026 , a three-year-old tigress, identified as T138 , was released into Buxa Tiger Reserve.   
 It was translocated from Valmiki Tiger Reserve, Bihar , marking the beginning of the phased tiger reintroduction programme.   
 The tigress subsequently moved into Assam and was captured by forest personnel using a tranquilliser dart.   
 It was brought back to Buxa on 4 November 2026 .   
 Tiger Augmentation and Recovery Programme   
 The tiger recovery initiative in Buxa has been implemented by the West Bengal Government with support from the NTCA and the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) .   
 The collaborative recovery project has been underway since 2018 .   
 Major interventions include:   
 Prey-base augmentation: More than 800 chital have been released to improve prey availability.   
 Habitat restoration: Approximately 380 hectares of grassland have been restored or converted over the past eight years.   
 Scientific monitoring: Camera traps and telemetry are used to monitor tiger movement and population recovery.   
 Protection measures: Strengthening anti-poaching activities and forest protection.   
 Community participation: Engagement of 64 Eco-Development Committees and Joint Forest Management Committees.   
 The programme aims to complement natural tiger recovery through scientifically guided interventions.   
 Why Buxa Tiger Reserve Was Selected for Tiger Reintroduction   
 Buxa experienced a prolonged absence of a stable resident tiger population due to:   
 Habitat degradation and fragmentation.   
 Changes in land use.   
 Decline in prey availability.   
 Increasing anthropogenic pressure.   
 The reserve has ecological connectivity with Bhutan and adjoining forest landscapes of Assam .   
 Camera-trap evidence has indicated natural tiger movement through the wider landscape, including an individual matched with a tiger from Manas Tiger Reserve, Assam , in 2023.   
 About Buxa Tiger Reserve   
 Location: Alipurduar district, West Bengal.   
 Established as a Tiger Reserve: 1983, under Project Tiger.   
 Area: Approximately 760.87 sq. km.   
 Geographical significance: Located in the eastern Himalayan foothills and the Dooars region.   
 Ecological connectivity: Linked with forest landscapes of Bhutan and Assam.   
 Major rivers: Sankosh, Raidak, Jayanti and Torsa are associated with the wider landscape.   
 Vegetation: Tropical moist and dry deciduous forests, along with other forest types.   
 Important wildlife: Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, leopard, gaur and several other species.   
 About Project Tiger   
 Launch: 1 April 1973.   
 Nodal Ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC).   
 Objective: Conservation of tigers and their habitats through protected areas, habitat management, anti-poaching measures and scientific monitoring.   
 National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA): Statutory body constituted under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, through the 2006 amendment.   
 The programme follows a landscape-based conservation approach , emphasising habitat connectivity, prey availability and community participation.

 Ease of Used Vehicle Ownership in India 
 Star marking (1-5) indicates the importance of topic -->
 Why in News?   
 The Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI) 2026 , released by Minister of State for Road Transport and Highways Harsh Malhotra on 4 November 2026, has highlighted significant differences among Indian states in the ease of buying, selling and transferring ownership of used vehicles.    
 Key Points:   
 State Rankings in the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index   
 Top-performing states:   
 1st: Andhra Pradesh.   
 2nd: Kerala.   
 3rd: Tamil Nadu.   
 Other notable rankings:   
 Delhi: 4th position.   
 Karnataka: 5th position.   
 Followed by Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana.   
 Lowest-ranked states:   
 West Bengal.   
 Bihar.   
 Uttar Pradesh (Last).   
 Key observation: No state scored more than six out of ten, indicating widespread structural challenges in used-vehicle ownership transfers.   
 About the Ease of Vehicle Ownership Index (EVOI) 2026   
 Prepared by: IndiaTech.org and Consumer VOICE.   
 Released by: Minister of State for Road Transport and Highways Harsh Malhotra.   
 Coverage: 15 states, accounting for more than 85% of India's organised used-car market .   
 Six assessment parameters:   
 Clarity of ownership transfer rules: Consistency and transparency of state-level procedures.   
 Digital infrastructure: Availability and reliability of online systems.   
 Procedural efficiency: Speed, predictability and administrative burden.   
 Fee transparency: Clarity of charges, application tracking and grievance redressal.   
 Consumer protection: Dealer support and trade infrastructure.   
 Actual transfer cost: Difference between prescribed government fees and the total amount paid by consumers.   
 Major Challenges in Used-Vehicle Ownership Transfer   
 High transaction costs:   
 The report identified cost as the weakest component of the used-vehicle ownership ecosystem.   
 Twelve out of 15 states scored below 3.5 in this parameter.   
 Manual verification, notary requirements, vehicle inspections and multiple departmental approvals increase costs.   
 Informal payments and intermediary dependence:   
 Actual ownership-transfer expenses can be nearly 10 times the statutory fee .   
 In Muzaffarpur, Bihar, a single transfer reportedly costs ₹13,000–14,000 over and above the prescribed VAHAN fee.   
 At Hosur and Krishnagiri in Tamil Nadu, an official fee of approximately ₹800 can increase to ₹7,000–8,000.   
 Delays in RC transfer:   
 Andhra Pradesh reportedly completes registration certificate (RC) transfers in approximately 7–10 days .   
 In Uttar Pradesh, the process can take more than 30 days .   
 In 13 of the 15 states assessed, applicants submit documents online but are still required to provide physical copies to the RTO.   
 Inter-state road tax differences:   
 Road tax varies significantly across states.   
 For a petrol car worth ₹6 lakh, the tax ranges from approximately 3% in Uttar Pradesh to 14% in Karnataka .   
 Only Andhra Pradesh and Telangana were reported to have functional refund mechanisms for vehicles transferred out of the state.   
 Existing Legal Framework for Ownership Transfer   
 Motor Vehicles Act, 1988:   
 Section 50 governs the transfer of ownership of motor vehicles.   
 It requires the transferor and transferee to report and complete the ownership-transfer process with the registering authority.   
 Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989:   
 Rule 55 prescribes the procedure and documents for transfer of ownership.   
 Form 29: Notice of transfer of ownership by the seller.   
 Form 30: Application for transfer of ownership by the purchaser.   
 Form 31: Transfer of ownership in favour of a legal heir following the death of the registered owner.   
 Form 32: Transfer of ownership in the case of a vehicle purchased through public auction.   
 Time limits for normal sale:   
 For a vehicle registered within the same state, the purchaser must apply for transfer within 14 days .   
 For a vehicle registered outside the state, the purchaser must apply within 45 days .   
 An applicable No Objection Certificate (NOC) and other prescribed documents are required for inter-state transfers.   
 Other important documents: Registration Certificate (RC), insurance certificate and applicable transfer fees.   
 India's Used-Vehicle Market   
 Market valuation: India's pre-owned vehicle market was valued at approximately US$36.4 billion in 2024–25 .   
 Projected market size: Expected to reach US$73.5 billion by 2030 .   
 Used-to-new vehicle sales ratio:   
 Currently approximately 1.3:1 .   
 Projected to increase to 1.7:1 by 2030 .   
 First-time buyers: Approximately 60–65% of used-vehicle buyers are first-time car owners.   
 Average used-car selling price: Increased from ₹4.49 lakh in 2021 to ₹5.47 lakh in 2025.   
 The growth of the sector is associated with affordability, lower upfront costs and expanding access to personal mobility .
